abstract_sentences.text: Probabilistic programming offers a powerful framework for modeling uncertainty, yet statistical model discovery in this domain entails navigating an immense search space under strict domain-specific constraints.

evidence.anchor: statistical model discovery ... immense search space under strict domain-specific constraints

abstract_sentences.text: When small language models are tasked with generating probabilistic programs, they frequently produce outputs that suffer from both syntactic, and semantic errors, such as flawed inference constructs.

evidence.anchor: small language models ... syntactic, and semantic errors

abstract_sentences.text: Motivated by probabilistic programmers’ domain expertise and debugging strategies, we introduce RefineStat, a language model–driven framework that enforces semantic constraints ensuring synthesized programs contain valid distributions, well-formed parameters, and then applies diagnostic-aware refinement by resampling prior or likelihood components whenever reliability checks fail.

evidence.anchor: semantic constraints ... diagnostic-aware refinement by resampling prior or likelihood components

abstract_sentences.text: We evaluate RefineStat on multiple probabilistic-programming code-generation tasks using smaller language models (SLMs) and find that it produces programs that are both syntactically sound and statistically reliable, often matching or surpassing those from closed-source large language models (e.g., OpenAI o3).

evidence.anchor: syntactically sound and statistically reliable, often matching or surpassing
Our code is available at https://github.com/structuredllm/RefineStat

final_judgment.single_storyline: RefineStat combines fragment-level semantic pruning with Bayesian-diagnostic-guided prior/likelihood resampling, then maximizes ELPD only within a reliability-filtered candidate set (p.3–6, Definitions 2–4 and Algorithm 1).
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main text keeps the workflow figure, six predicates, seven-score acceptance rule, zeta=5, Algorithm 1, Tables 1–6, and the GP diagnostic conflict that distinguishes trustworthy posterior sampling from a high but unreliable ELPD (p.3–10).
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Prompt/data arrays, metric definitions, thresholds, hardware, failure taxonomy, token cost, and memorization variants move to p.15–24; these are needed for reproduction and for judging the efficiency boundary (Appendix D–G).
final_judgment.best_pattern: The strongest pattern is to operationalize reliability as explicit indicators and a valid model space, pair a tiny sd-to-sigma example with the semantic predicate, and use a high-ELPD/bad-diagnostics counterexample to motivate the selection order (p.4–5, p.7).
final_judgment.largest_gap: The title promises efficient exploration although Appendix G.1 reports a 1.9x average token ratio and no wall-clock/dollar cost; significance language lacks a test, several counts conflict internally, and global optimality/full Bayesian adequacy remain open (p.10, p.23).
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For reliable generation, formalize static legality, runtime/sampling health, and predictive selection as separate checks, and include a counterexample showing why a single final score is insufficient; expose cost denominators and failure definitions alongside the headline metric.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule fits executable DSLs with observable diagnostics and a defined candidate score. It cannot establish global optimality or adequacy when prior/posterior predictive judgment is manual or domain-specific; those require additional evidence beyond B(M) (p.10 Limitations).
